Our full-year revenue of $15 billion from sales and trading rose 17%, and we generated more than $7 billion of investment banking revenues this year, an increase of 27% over last year. Investment in brokerage revenue grew 5% to nearly $15 billion. Our expenses were higher as a result of the many costs associated with COVID and the support for our teams, our clients, and our communities we serve. For a comparison of 2019 and 2020, 2020 included the third quarter addition of merchant service costs following dissolution of joint venture in the third quarter of 2019. These costs were always incurred as a net revenue deduction under joint venture accounting, but now come through our expense line. Setting aside the net elevated COVID-related expense and a change in accounting for merchant services, our teams continue to do a good job managing costs, and you'll see that later, and Paul will talk about it, and maintain a focus on using productivity gains to fund all the investments we're making across the franchise, and including increasing client flows. With $36 billion of excess capital above our common CET1 minimum requirements and excess capital above the SLR reverting back to its normal calculation and completion of the CCAR exam, we'll once again begin repurchasing shares starting today. As you know, our first priority for use of all our capital is to grow our business organically, and we have funded growth in many areas. We have funded and expanded minimum wages to $20 an hour for all our teammates. We expanded and increased COVID benefits, and we've taken care of all that. Now we're looking to return as much capital to our shareholders as we're allowed and as our board deems prudent. So you saw this morning at the beginning of that in a separate press release that our board has approved share repurchase in the first quarter of up to $3.2 billion, including shares issued to employees. This is in addition to maintaining our quarterly dividend at 18 cents per quarter, and that accounts for the return of another $1.6 billion of capital. This is the maximum allowed under the Fed's guidelines established for the first quarter of 2021. Beyond the first quarter, when we find out what the rules are, we'll continue to change our authorizations to reflect those rules. Our companies are highly liquid and generally in pretty good shape, except, of course, for those industries that are focused on our most hard hit by COVID.

We saw record sign-ons through our Cash Pro app. This is the way a commercial customer accesses an app in commercial cash management businesses. Expenses increased driven by revenue-related expense and investments in our sales force. Merrill Lynch and the private bank both continue to grow households as we remain a provider of choice for affluent clients. Client balances rose to a record of more than $3.3 trillion. Up $302 billion year over year, driven by higher market levels as well as positive client flows. Let's move to our global banking results on slide 20. COVID has also heavily impacted global banking through lower interest rates, softer loan demand, and higher credit costs. But here again, we saw improvement. The business earned nearly $1.7 billion in Q4, improving $751 million from Q3, driven by lower provision expense and improved revenue. On a year-over-year basis, earnings were $341 million lower, driven by NII. Looking at revenue and comparing to Q3, revenue improvement was driven by higher investment banking fees as well as more leasing activity associated with our clients' ESG investments. Investment banking fees for the company of nearly $1.9 billion grew 5% from Q3 and were up 26% year-over-year. As Brian noted, this performance led to improved market share overall and in a number of key products. Provision expense reflected a reserve release of $266 million in Q4 compared to a build in reserves of $555 million in Q3. Non-interest expense was higher compared to the linked quarter and year-over-year, primarily reflecting investments in the platform as well as support for the PPP program and also reflecting the recording of merchant services expense given the change in accounting versus the year-ago quarter. As Brian noted earlier, customers continued to appreciate the ease, safety, and convenience of our digital banking capabilities, and usage continued to grow, helping defray other costs. We present some digital highlights on slide 22. As noted earlier, loans declined but saw stabilization late in the quarter. And continuing the trend since Q2, the spread of the loan portfolio continued to tick higher as spreads of new originations on average exceeded the average spread of the portfolio. Average deposits increased 26% relative to Q3 as businesses remained highly liquid. Okay, switching to global markets. On slide 23, results reflect solid year-over-year improvement in revenue from sales and trading, but a decline from the robust levels of Q3. As I usually do, I will talk about segment results excluding DVA. This quarter, net DVA was a small loss of $56 million. On that basis, global markets produced $834 million of earnings in Q4, a decline from the more robust trading in Q3, but up markedly from Q4-19. Focusing on year-over-year, revenue was up 13% on higher sales and trading. The year-over-year expense increase was driven by higher activity-based costs for both trading and unemployment claims processing. Sales and trading contributed $3.1 billion to revenue, increasing 7% year-over-year, driven by a 30% improvement in equities and a 5% decline in FIP. The strength in equities was driven by market volatility and investment repositioning, which drove client activity higher. The decline in FIC reflected strong credit trading performance, which was more than offset by declines across most macro products and mortgage trading. As Brian noted, the year-over-year performance of this business has been strong in every quarter of 2020. You can see that on slide 24. And that produced strong segment returns of 15% on allocated capital for the year. OK. Finally, on slide 25, we show all other which reported a loss of $425 million. Compared to Q3, the decline in net income was driven primarily by the prior quarter's tax benefit of $700 million associated with our UK deferred tax asset. Revenue declined from Q3 driven by the accounting for wind and solar and other ESG investments. We also experienced some modest equity investment losses. Expenses declined from Q3 on lower litigation expense, but were partially offset by higher marketing costs. For 2021, absent any changes in the current tax laws or unusual items, we would expect the effective tax rate to be in the low double digits driven by the level of ESG client activity relative to pre-tax earnings. And with that, I'll turn it back to Lee and Brian for Q&A.

speakers.speaker: spk08
speakers.text: And at this time, if you'd like to ask a question, please press the star and one on your touchtone phone. That's star and one on your touchtone phone. We'll take our first question today from John McDonald with Autonomous Research. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk20
speakers.text: Hi, good morning. I wanted to ask a question on expenses. Brian mentioned expecting the cost number to be flattish in 2021 versus 2020. Just kind of wondering, is that all in expenses, Paul, or some kind of core metric to give an outlook for the expenses that you expect and the COVID trend for COVID expenses this year? Thanks.

speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: Yeah, John, that's all in, given the around $55 billion both years. And so we feel good about the ability to keep bringing down COVID. It came out a little slower this quarter, largely due to the fact that you go back and think where we were in October on case counts, the need to continue to provide strong benefits to our teammates, including, you know, the child care in their homes so they could be effective. That's why we get those customer scores and why You know, the growth in checking sales was 70%, 80% of a normal year. Again, we have to, you know, 40% of branches closed. So, yeah, flat year-over-year, all-in number, and then we're working the dynamics underneath it. But importantly, remember, we are investing $3.5 billion in technology next year, you know, new financial centers, expansion, employees to help sell more, and, you know, we'll continue to drive it through. So you'll see sort of a change in the COVID cost coming down, hopefully, as we move through the year.

speakers.speaker: spk20
speakers.text: But we've got some work to do, but flat year over year overall. Okay. And then longer term, Brian, you've talked about getting back to a low $54 billion as kind of a run rate, ex-COVID. Is that still how you're thinking about things?

speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: Yeah, we should start to work down. Again, as we said many years ago, as we get out in the out years and get more and more efficient, the – The day-to-day, you know, the quotidian cost of, you know, rent increases and, you know, payroll pay increases work at you. But the idea is to, you know, have the net expense grow sort of at 1% a year. So 3% up from just day-to-day cost to manage a couple percents out. And so we'll continue to work that down in the future. We've got work to do on getting these COVID expenses out of here. Okay, thanks.

speakers.speaker: spk08
speakers.text: Our next question comes from Mike Mayo with Wells Fargo. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk07
speakers.text: Hi. I also wanted to follow up on the efficiency. I mean, you're making big strides with digital banking in so many ways with 39 million digital households are engaged. And you go through all those metrics and you see efficiency ratio for the quarter of 69%. And if you take out your 400 million of COVID costs, maybe it would be 67%. But that's still a far cry from the 57% to 59% where you had been. Now, I know low rates hurt a little bit, but either you're investing more than you've disclosed, or there's some other COVID costs in there, or you're not becoming more efficient, as you said in your opening comments, Brian. So help me kind of reconcile your current efficiency or my adjusted efficiency ratio with a more normal level.

speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: So, Mike, I take you back to page 11 on the net interest yield and net interest income and realize that, you know, basically in the four quarters of last year, we lost $2 billion of revenue per quarter, which is the bridge from, you know, a lot of that bridge. And so as we work that back up and ultimately as rates rise at $2 billion, that's per quarter. So $8 billion in revenue was really no cost. you know, that'll go up. So we continue to get more efficient in the branches. The cost of operating over the deposit base is now at $135,000. And, you know, we added $700,000 of checking accounts. So, you know, you're right, but it's more affected by the revenue impact to NI than it is by anything else in terms of expenses. Remember, we're saying net COVID cost of, you know, $300,000, $400,000. That includes offsetting against that all savings of travel and stuff. The gross costs are obviously much higher than We've got about just we opened up PPP today. We've got 5,000 employees ready to go to complete the next round of PPP and the forgiveness process. And, you know, as that finishes off, that stuff will come out of the system. So we've got you.

speakers.speaker: spk07
speakers.text: And then the follow-up to that is going to NII. I'm not sure if you gave a specific outlook or not, Paul, when you went through that. I mean, as you said, liquidity is now greater than loans. your loan-to-deposit ratio at close to 50%. I think it's the lowest in history, like ever, right now. So there's a lot of dry powder there. But did you give guidance for NII for this year, assuming the four-year yield curve stays where it is? And do you think you can somehow pull out positive operating leverage this year, or is that too tough given the rate environment?

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: We didn't give specific guidance. I can give you a little more color on our perspective on 2021. But I do think as you think about how you want to estimate and model NAI and how it may unfold in 21, I think it's really sort of helpful to kind of review the progress we made in 2020. There's a lot of clues there. Remember in Q1 of 20, interest rates fell to historically low levels. Short rates were down 150 and long rates were down 100 basis points, plus loans declined significantly beginning in Q2 as demand weakened and larger companies assessed the capital markets, paid down debt, and built liquidity. In the past, when we've had situations like this where interest rates and or loans have declined, it's always taken sort of several quarters to reach a point where renewed balance sheet growth was significant enough to compensate. We believe we found that NAI bottom in Q3, and NAI indeed moved higher in Q4. All else equal, day count, et cetera, it should become easier from here to grow NAI. I think what helped us to start to grow again quickly in this crisis was the tremendous influx of deposits and our relatively recent confidence to invest the excess in securities instead of holding that excess in cash. So our continued investment of that cash in Q4 leads us to believe that, you know, we can offset the headwinds of low loan demand in the near term, you know, reinvestment yields, and two less days of NAI in Q1, leaving NAI relatively flat in Q1 versus Q4 before moving up through the balance of the year. Remember, in Q2 and Q3, we picked back up those days of interest we lost in Q1. As Brian reviewed, we also saw commercial loans stabilize at the end of Q4, providing hope that increased loan demand will soon follow. Given that we expect some loan demand through the year and using the existing rate curve, which has steepened over the past 90 days, we would expect NAI in Q421, for example, to be much higher than Q121. And when we get to the second half of 21, year-over-year quarterly comparisons to 2020, as well as the second half of 21 compared to the first half of 20, should be quite favorable.

speakers.speaker: spk07
speakers.text: OK, that's helpful. And when you say a lot higher in Q4 than Q1, bigger than a bread box or, I mean, any sizings of that?

speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: Once we get to, Paul, the simple way to think about it, Mike, is once you sort of get underneath the levels, you know, you start growing the loan growth, and we've said we'll outgrow the economy and loan growth in normalized times, and that feeds in on us. But we've got to work it back up from here. It's a four- or five-quarter fight to kind of get this huge balance sheet turned and just fight it down and then have it grow back out. So we'll see.

speakers.speaker: spk07
speakers.text: Okay, thank you.

speakers.speaker: spk08
speakers.text: And our next question is from Glenn Shore with Evercore. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: Hi, thanks very much. You guys are pretty predictable and steady on this front, but I'm curious on your thoughts on capital. I'm not sure your CT1 has ever been higher. and your requirements are not going up. So as capital continues to build and your G-SID target is reasonably low relative to your big peers, just what are you thinking in terms of how aggressive you get on the capital return versus we don't talk much about bulk on acquisitions with you, but curious how you think about that and if you might address asset management in particular given your great distribution franchise.

speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: Then let's go backwards to that one, you know, the big leverage point would be more deposit acquisitions and markets we're not in and stuff like that, but we can't do it. It's illegal and has been for, you know, all the way back since GLBA or whatever it was, you know, 20, 30 years ago, so even before. And then, you know, asset management. Remember, we sold asset management because we believed that being the large distributor industry, is the priority. So don't expect us, we look at stuff from time to time like everybody does, but the way we built this company was organic growth and then delivering the capital back to the shareholders. And what's interesting, you know, We'll see what the rules change, but remember that things like the SLR and the accommodations that were given, we didn't need. We have plenty of SLR. It doesn't have any constraint. It doesn't become an issue. Like you said, even if you look at the SEB recalcs and stuff, we got plenty over that. So we will be aggressive on returning capital. We got basically two months to return those $3 billion and change. We got to return now, and then we'll see what happens. what the Fed instructions are, and then we'll get after it as we move forward. And we look at things from time to time, but there just isn't much to consider in the United States right now. And the best answer is to develop, continue development of this franchise on an organic basis. And it works. You know, if you look in the markets, we've expanded our brand system to, we're averaging $100 million or more in deposits per branch, and the ones have been open a couple years. And, you know, moving share up, you know, literally year by year by year. And so we think that's where we've got to keep driving.

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: I appreciate all that. Is there a specific either buffer above the CT1 and or you want to put it in the 36 billion excess? Where's a natural resting ground? Not tomorrow, but just whenever you get there.

speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: Yeah, we always said sort of 50 basis points, you know, above the relevant binding criteria is where you'd start to slow down. But remember, we're basically only getting back to earnings, and so we've got a lot of room between us and whatever the requirement is plus 50 basis points. And from time to time, those move around, advance to standardized, you know, SLR, whatever's binding. But think about that's where the board targets are.

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: Excellent. Thanks for all that, Mark.

speakers.speaker: spk08
speakers.text: Our next question is from Matt O'Connor with Deutsche Bank. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk10
speakers.text: Good morning. Can you talk a bit about the timing of the liquidity deployment in the fourth quarter? I think mortgage rates actually came down. And, you know, one could argue if you look out six to 12 months, longer-term rates will be higher as kind of vaccines get rolled out, the economy picks up. So Obviously, you have tons of deposits, but it's also pretty long duration assets, I would think, that you're buying. So you could talk about that.

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: Yeah, you're absolutely right. The 10-year was up in the quarter, but rates on mortgage-backed securities, well, certainly mortgage rates to customers declined, and rates on mortgage-backed securities, I think, declined slightly. Having said that, we're always going to balance liquidity, capital, and you know returns and profits and we did deploy and as we said on our third quarter call approximately a hundred million of our cash and securities it went into both mortgage-backed securities and some treasuries in the quarter and we you know we think that was the right thing to do we understand the rate structure we did get probably an improvement on our yield on that $100 billion of approximately 125 basis points. And I would say we've still got a lot of excess cash, Matt. If you look at our balance sheet, cash grew by $70 to $80 billion this quarter. I mean, that was the growth on top of what we already had, net of deployment. So we still have a lot of room to invest in the future. And we plan to do some more investments in Q2, but we're obviously always looking at the right environment.

speakers.speaker: spk14
speakers.text: Say Liberty Mutual customizes your car insurance so you only pay for what you need. Oh boy. Only pay for what you need.

speakers.speaker: spk10
speakers.text: And then I guess somewhat related, you know, is there a point where you just say we don't want some of these deposits? You know, it's better to kind of free up even more capital or just have a little bit more of an efficient balance sheet and not have to kind of make some of these tough decisions or charge for the deposits?

speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: Well, so if a customer comes to you to open a checking account and start a lifetime relationship, You'd never turn that down, whether it's a commercial customer or a consumer customer for core deposits. And so if you look at the growth, you know, we're not bidding for CDs and money markets on the consumer side. You can see that $108 billion to $160 billion was checking account balance growth. And, by the way, when rates rose before, we continued our checking account growth, you know, and we expect that continues. These are core customer relationships. So go back and look as rates rose, you know, 16, 17, 18. We continued to grow checking and double-digit, you know, type of numbers quarter after quarter after quarter, which means you're just taking market share. And so on the commercial side, the same thing, the GTS business. We are not out in the market taking, you know, You have short-term deposits from people who haven't been, and so this is all real core stuff that we're getting paid to take, and albeit it gets sandwiched a little bit as the zero floors are hit in the commercial side, frankly, that services overcome the zero floor, but you'd be hard-pressed to turn it down. So it's not like we have a lot of, you know, here's a few billion dollars. Can you put it on your balance? That just doesn't happen. We don't do that. We turn that down already.

speakers.speaker: spk10
speakers.text: Okay, thank you.

speakers.speaker: spk08
speakers.text: Our next question is from Betsy Gracek with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk15
speakers.text: Hey, thanks. Paul, just first off, a follow-on question to the last one around the reinvestment into securities. Like you mentioned, you did $92 billion or so this past quarter. So as we're thinking about the NII guidance you just gave, should we be anticipating an increase into the securities book that's above and beyond that roughly 100 million run rate that you did in 4Q?

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: Look, we continue to assess assess the excess deposits, and we do expect to continue to deploy more cash into securities. We're not really planning on disclosing how much more, but there is a meaningful amount in that guidance that we gave you. The size and pace of the purchases are obviously going to be influenced by a number of judgments, including things like expected loan demand and customer deposit behavior. So, yeah, I mean, I'm not going to give you a number, but it's a meaningful increase that we're expecting to do in Q2, excuse me, in this quarter.

speakers.speaker: spk15
speakers.text: Yeah, okay, got it. And then just separately in talking about credit, you know, you indicated that the delinquencies are suggesting that your NCOs are going to be coming down Q1Q and 2Q. And, you know, that's a pretty stunning statement given that, you know, we still have this unemployment rate where it is. Can you just talk a little bit about what, you know, why you expect that's happening in your book of business? Do you just have a population that's really not being impacted by the unemployment rate? Maybe you could give us some color there.

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: Sure. Now, I want to correct. I think I heard you say something that you may not have said, but I want to make sure everybody heard it. We expect NCOs for CARD to be up in... it's not going to be down in Q1.

speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: And the reason for that... Hey, Paul, we lost you there for a second just as you said what you were saying.

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: Okay, sorry. What I wanted to make sure everybody heard, because I thought I heard you say something different. We expect a charge-off for card, which, you know, obviously the primary driver of consumer losses. We expect those to be up in Q1 and then decline in Q2. And, you know...

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: The uptick in... Yeah, that's what I thought I said, so sorry about that.

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: Okay. And that expectation is being driven by what we see in the 90-plus bucket in terms of delinquencies. And those delinquencies that have sort of a... If you look at the other buckets, you'll see in the 90-plus bucket, they're higher than the other bucket. And that's the deferrals. They've worked their way from the 5-day to 30-day the 30 to 60 day they're now in the 90 bucket and we can look back historically and say X percent of our delinquencies in the 90 bucket show up as losses in the next quarter because you get to 180 days and so that's all we're seeing but importantly when you look behind the 90 day bucket you don't see the same elevated levels in fact if you look at the 30 day bucket you're down meaningfully year over year in terms of levels. So that's why we think Q2 will have to come down. Probably maybe half too strong of a word. All else equal, you would think it would come down. And the question is really, if you think about it, the people who have been affected by this health crisis, who are unemployed, who have been helped by stimulus, will this new stimulus carry them to the point where they get vaccinated and they get jobs back? And will we ever see those losses, or will they just be pushed out into future periods?

speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: So that's just to give you some extra information we included. If you look at page 27 of the deck in the appendix, And the four charts at the bottom were put in specifically because of this question we knew would arise. So if you look across the buckets and you look from the mid-19 to the end of 20, you can see the different delinquency buckets are all down. Even the 90-plus day is down in gross dollar amount year over year. But you can see that what people thought was sort of the The analogy of a pig through a snake is probably more of a mouse through the snake. And at one up, it's still a lower dollar amount. And then it would come back down because you move from the left to the right side of the page. And if you go back to page 14, you can actually see in the top chart that the total charge-offs in consumer this quarter were 482. If you look in the red bars, which is a credit card, you can see that they're down dramatically year over year. in terms of gross dollar amounts, and then this will bode well in the future. So when we talk about going back up, they're going up from a level that was much below where they have ever been historically in terms of dollar amounts. And so the last point you made, just so you have it, is that the unemployment rate in our customer base is below the unemployment rate in American society, and that's just due to the especially on the borrowing customer base due to the client selection and being in the prime business.

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: Hey, Betsy, maybe just to complete the conversation with respect to commercial, you know, we have seen increases in reservable criticized, but they haven't, you know, we haven't seen MPLs increase significantly. They're at 45 basis points of loans right now. So we think commercial losses in future quarters are going to be driven by really company-specific events that play out over the coming quarters and will obviously likely be concentrated in industries more heavily impacted by COVID. I would point out that in this quarter, we took some losses as we chose to reduce exposures in industries that were affected by COVID, and that, you know, crystallized some losses and showed up on our NCOs this quarter. If we hadn't take those losses, we would have, hadn't sold those credits, we would have had even lower NCOs in commercial.

speakers.speaker: spk15
speakers.text: Yep. Yep. No, I get it. I mean, you know, we're forecasting NCOs peaking sometime in, you know, the end of 2020. one, but given your comments, maybe the question is, have they already peaked or will they have peaked for you in one queue?

speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: The care there is to think the consumer is really, at this point, sort of run the course in the commercial. The reserves are built and the activity may occur in the out-quarters, but the consumer runs the course by just straight throughput, 5 to 30, 30 to 60, 60 to 90. We're showing you the charts that really tell you what's going to happen in the first half because it's a pretty mathematical calculation.

speakers.speaker: spk15
speakers.text: Yep, I got it. Impressive. Thank you.

speakers.speaker: spk08
speakers.text: Next question from Vivek Junaidu with J.D. Morgan. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: Hey, Brian. Hey, Paul. Brian, I have a question for you. Can you talk a little bit about You're fixed trading. You've lost share in 2020, including in 4Q. What are you thinking about this business? What are your plans for it?

speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: Well, our plans are to keep running it the way we do. And if you look at it year over year, you know, it's an integrated business market. Jimmy does a good job. It's up, you know, we showed you on that chart, you know, it's up. It's one of the highest years it's ever had, 15% or whatever it is up year over year. So they do a great job. We don't play in certain areas which run on a given quarter. Interestingly enough, when they don't run, people forget about that. And so we have more of a stable level of revenue. So if you look on page 24, you'll see that 13.2, 13.3, 12.9, 15.2. So we had a... a good year, and the FIC was up from 8.4 to 9.7 in revenue, which is substantial, and some of the areas we don't trade in. So we're more credit-driven, and that's what drives us versus some of the competitors. We're happy with the business. They do a great job, and it's really there to help drive the connectivity between our issuing clients and our investing clients, and we'll continue to drive it.

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: Can I just add one point? Sure. You know, happy to sort of see what data you're looking at, but I don't think we're losing market share in FIC. I think we're actually gaining market share, perhaps not as much as we're gaining in equities, but we're gaining market share certainly in the segments where we're investing within FIC.

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: Paul, your growth rates have been below peers, so are you doing that by segment of business like Brian was talking about and parsing that out between commodities and macro and and credit products, or is it something else? Because certainly if you look at year-on-year growth rates, you've been below your peers through several quarters in 2020.

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: Some of the peers, but not all of the peers.

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: Right. Lots of peers in Europe. Right, the bigger ones.

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: Yeah, but... Yeah, I guess... If you look at global fee pools, you'll see that we are gaining market share in FIC.

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: Okay. Okay, we'll go back and compare with the Europeans. Different question, Paul, for you. MBS premium amortization expense, how much, what was that this quarter?

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: I don't think we're giving the exact number, but it was up and it did impact, I would say, meaningfully NII. You know, from here, we're going to need to see mortgage, customer mortgage rates, you know, stabilize and go higher for that number to stabilize and go lower. I'll give you this sense of its impact, though. If you look at the decline in net interest yield for the company, a third of it was due to premium amortization in the quarter.

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: And so by the time the fourth quarter guide that you were giving us for NII to be much better, how much of a reversal are you forecasting in that NBS premium amortization in that guide?

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: Well, I would look at the forward rates for you to estimate that. We're not assuming that it goes up. in that guidance because if you look at the forward curve, rates by the end of the year are up from where they are today.

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: My question was how much are you expecting it to decline, Paul?

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: I understand you're asking for the dollar amount and I'm not going to give you the dollar amount.

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: Not the dollar amount but any sense of percentage since you said one third of the of the decline came from that? Any sense of, you know, I'm not asking for precise relevant, I'm not expecting that, but any sense?

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: Maybe we can follow up. I mean, I don't have it off the top of my head. I could probably give you some sense of how much, what percent of the improvement is from that, but I just don't have it off the top of my head. The other thing that I would point out, just to keep in mind as you're thinking about the write-off of premium, is that it's not just at this point due to the decline in rates. You have to remember that the portfolio has gotten bigger too.

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: Right. But you've been hurt more than others by it, so obviously that should turn around for you later in the year if refines start to slow.

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: That's a meaningful sort of tailwind if mortgage rates increase.

speakers.speaker: spk10
speakers.text: All right.

speakers.speaker: spk08
speakers.text: Thanks. Next question is from Ken Houston with Jefferies. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk11
speakers.text: Thanks. Good morning. Just one accounting follow-up for you, Paul. You mentioned the low double-digit tax rate and that other feline for where the ESG investments go through has been pretty volatile, but a pretty big negative number. And I just wanted to see if there's any way you can help us understand just what that looks like when you're helping us understand, you know, the tax rate as a, as the other side of it.

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: Yeah, sure. I can, I can try to help you with that. I guess there's two ways to triangulate on it. The look at the other income line for the company. Okay. And with respect to modeling that line, it's going to bounce around a lot quarter to quarter. speakers.speaker: spk08

speakers.speaker: spk02
speakers.text: Hey, good morning. Maybe just a little bit on consumer loan growth. It seems like you deliberately shrunk residential mortgage. Auto looked pretty good. But credit card was a little sluggish, I think, given typical seasonality. So, you know, customers are flush with cash. How do we think about the demand for lending going forward? speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: Well, let me just, you know, the issue was if you think about being a large consumer lender and especially you watch you on Secured Space, you know, when March, April, May hit, you pulled in, And, you know, even in a small business space. So the good news is that we're reverting to norm. And so in December, for example, we had, you know, 198,000 booked accounts in credit card. speakers.speaker: spk02
speakers.text: So is the uptick in marketing spend sort of reflective of that push to re-engage with consumer, and we should expect some nice sort of improvement going forward?

speakers.speaker: spk02
speakers.text: Okay, great. Thank you.

speakers.speaker: spk08
speakers.text: Our next question is from Gerard Cassidy with RBC Capital Markets. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk21
speakers.text: Good morning, Brian. Good morning, Paul. Hi. Brian, just to follow up on that consumer commentary you gave and in your prepared remarks, I think you said that you brought your underwriting, you're bringing your underwriting standards back to the pre-COVID levels. Two questions, I guess, or two parts to it. Can you give us some color of how they changed, you know, when you tightened them up, now they're back to normal? Was it FICO scores on the consumer side? speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: Yeah, so let me start with the commercial side. And this is about sort of the relationship side of commercial business, business banking, global commercial banking, global corporate investment banking. Basically, in March 8th, we stopped prospecting, frankly, because it was sort of impossible to do. Plus, you want to make sure you understood the portfolios. We've done quarterly portfolio reviews, every single loan going through to make sure the ratings are right, make sure we understood what the customer did, make sure we understood whether they're going to need covenant waivers. Over the course of the time here, it's sort of the group of customers which are in industries that Paul talked about that are difficult, and the rest of the customers are solid and in good shape. In fact, frankly, their credit has been improving as we looked at it by quarter. And so about four months ago, we moved into prospecting with a very narrow list of prospects for business banking, commercial banking, think for middle market and upper end of small business across all our markets. With them, recently we flipped, and they can go back to full prospecting except for limited industries that you'd expect. On the small business side, because of the nature of the business, it was a little more dramatic, and we've opened back up. And we're getting, you know, we're up, I think, in the fourth quarter, to give you a sense. We were up, you know, 50% in terms of originations, you know, quarter over quarter, but we're still up a lot more than that, more than 50%. We're still down 50% year over year, up 100-plus%. and quarter-to-link quarter, I think. And so new commitments up 135% year-over-year, so down 47%. So that shows you that it's coming through, and we'll see that happen on the small business side. So that was probably the slowest because it's with the area of the most risk, and so that's the commercial side. When you go to the consumer side, the reality was we basically, you know, we stayed on LTVs on the commercial, on the consumer mortgage side, We basically stopped, you know, with the FICO requirements. We slowed down and do the market dynamics, you know, home equity slowed down. Auto, we went back out more quickly just because of the secure nature of it, short-term nature of it. So we felt good about that. And probably, you know, we were always super prime and stayed there. But it's really what's changed in consumer in the last, Several, you know, last few months has been the move, and we're back to probably 80%, 90% of the ability to generate that we had. We were down probably, you know, 20%, and we've moved back up, and so we'll see that flow through. But it was really just until you had some clarity where this thing was going, you had to be careful for a while. So that bodes well to economic activity and loan growth in the future.

speakers.speaker: spk21
speakers.text: Very good. Thank you. And then, Paul, in your comments, you were talking about having greater confidence with the deposits to go further out on the yield curve. speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: Sure. So what's changed is A, the level of deposits, right? We continue to get more and more deposits in. B, reviewing, as Brian noted earlier, where the deposits are coming from, predominantly high-quality deposits, checking, et cetera, new accounts. Three, when you look at just the sheer growth of the money supply, coupled with the expectation as we come out of this recession that the velocity of money will likely increase, it's hard to build a case that we're going to see a significant decline in deposits in the U.S. And we're going to get our fair share, if not more, of those deposits. So because of how we've run our business on both commercial and the retail side in terms of focusing on high-quality deposits. We just feel good about the deposits we have.

speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: Yeah, and Gerard, just to make it sort of straightforward, once you got by, you had the feeling that this was an ephemeral move, especially on the corporate side, that this was going to be a good way to stay with you. speakers.speaker: spk21
speakers.text: Very good. And Brian and Paul, hopefully we'll see you guys at BAB this year in person.

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: We'll try.

speakers.speaker: spk21

speakers.speaker: spk16
speakers.text: Yeah, thanks. I just have one question. It's regarding the reserve levels overall. speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: I'm not sure we give the exact but let me just give you a sense. If you take our reserve setting weighting, in other words, what we set the reserve by in December, for year-end 2020, because we set it before the statistics, the unemployment rate was 7.8%, and for year-end 2021, it was 6.6%, and obviously the actual was 100 basis points plus below that. So you would expect, as you have more confidence that the forward path is into a narrow range in the forward probability, two things are going to happen as you go forward. One is the sheer dollar volumes of activity has changed, and so you're dealing with less in terms of charge-offs and things like that, which gives you confidence of where the path is. But most importantly, as you think about real reserve setting and lifetime reserves, is that the economic assumptions are clarifying and the end of the COVID era is clarifying with the vaccine. And as we see that, you'll see the uncertainty come down pretty quickly on the other side of that, when that shows up in our assumptions. So we're, we waited, you know, downside, nearly 50% of the elements that waiting will come down over time. And so when that comes down over time, you'll, you'll see the reserves releases come away from that. The second thing is as the duration of the rest of the crisis comes in, with more certainty, i.e., more people vaccinated, you also see the lifetime calculation include the other side of the river to a bigger, bigger portion, and so that will drive it. So both those things will change it. And, you know, as Paul said earlier, you know, if you look at our underlying economics team, they have the economy crossing over. you know where it was before and growing past in terms of sheer size you know the end of this year and our reserve setting takes it into next year and things like that so so we are using a more conservative case which implies judgment okay great thanks we'll take today's last question from charles peabody with portalis please go ahead

speakers.speaker: spk05
speakers.text: The first deals with what's going on in the regulatory front. Recently, we just had two new potential appointees, one to the SEC and one to the CFPB. I'm wondering what sort of issues you thought might emerge with these appointees and more on the consumer side because that's what I'm hearing where the biggest push is going to be. Some of the things I'm hearing is there's going to be a crackdown on payday lending, overdraft fees, usurious rates, artificial intelligence used in redlining. Most of those probably affect overdraft fees, but are there anything you can think of that might affect you and specifically what sort of things might affect overdraft fees?

speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: Well, you know, a decade plus ago, we started changing before the rules were changed. Our posture in overdraft fee is realizing that a more stable customer base was vastly better for the franchise than the operating deficiency. And so, you know, we welcome an industry which has a great consumer base. oriented path to it because that's how we run our company. We've been doing it that way for a long time. So our fees on overdrafts have been declining. Uh, it really is a percentage of fees every year and probably in gross dollar amounts most years. And, and so we're not dependent on those largely because of how we run the business being court customer checks, 90%, uh, plus, uh, the primary checking account in the household. And therefore they, they tend to overdraft less than in this year with the stimulus and stuff. It's even, uh, It's even lower. So we welcome, we introduced this new loan product that basically gives a right to get an emergency loan for $5, and that is our response to allowing our customers who have been with us for a while to access their money for really no interest at all and use it in anticipation of paying us back quickly. These are things we've done to really help our retail customer segment, which is the mass market customer segment, manage their lives effectively. And so we don't have a business built in those kind of fee structures, and that's why we welcome any regulation that brings the market to us, because as the most efficient and the best brand and the best customer service, largest franchise, that's fine with us.

speakers.speaker: spk05
speakers.text: Thanks. And my follow-up question deals with FIC trading. You know, I recognize the fourth quarter on a historical basis was very, very strong. It would be a value for all banks. FIC trading revenues didn't. And so my question is, were you a little more conservative in the fourth quarter because you already had a year? Is there something... that's making it more difficult.

speakers.text: Charlie, you're really cutting out. This is Lee. You're really cutting out. I'm not sure we picked up. I think you were asking a question about FIC and something, but we couldn't hear you.

Morgan, at Citi, at Goldman, everybody. So I'm trying to understand, is there something in the environment that's changing that's making it more difficult to be too aggressive in their expectations?

Despite the fact we're investing heavily to have the best franchise. So thank you for your support. We look forward to talking to you next time. Thanks.

First, I wanted to provide some brief commentary on 2020 for the full year, then talk about what we see in the economy as we enter 2021, and then highlight some areas where I believe we made strong strategic progress that will drive momentum into 2021 and beyond. So starting on slide two, 2020 was a tough operating environment, as you all know. In that period, we generated net income of nearly $18 billion, or $1.87 in EPS, and earned a return above our cost of capital. Our EPS was down 32% compared to 2019, driven by the impacts of coronavirus pandemic on the company and the economy. As you know, the Fed dropped rates to nearly zero. Longer rates also fell to historic lows. Loan demand surged and then waned as the panic subsided. That reduced net interest income. But as we told you last quarter, that we believe that I'd likely bottomed in the third quarter of 2019. In fact, we saw a modest improvement this quarter, which Paul will cover later, despite the challenges from lower loans. Non-interest revenue declined slightly, but included some interesting dynamics, highlighting diversity of Bank of America's model. Consumer fees declined, driven by the activity levels of clients, but also by higher account balances and customer accounts. That's a good thing for the economy going forward. Our business mix allowed us to benefit from more market-related activities in sales and trading, investment banking, and investment brokerage in the wealth management businesses. Our full-year revenue of $15 billion from sales and trading rose 17%, and we generated more than $7 billion of investment banking revenues this year, an increase of 27% over last year. Investment in brokerage revenue grew 5% to nearly $15 billion. Our expenses were higher as a result of the many costs associated with COVID and the support for our teams, our clients, and our communities we serve. For a comparison of 2019 and 2020, 2020 included the third quarter addition of merchant service costs following dissolution of joint venture in the third quarter of 2019. These costs were always incurred as a net revenue deduction under joint venture accounting, but now come through our expense line. Setting aside the net elevated COVID-related expense and a change in accounting for merchant services, our teams continue to do a good job managing costs, and you'll see that later, and Paul will talk about it, and maintain a focus on using productivity gains to fund all the investments we're making across the franchise, and including increasing client flows. Expenses then remained relatively flat year over year. We expect them to be flat for 21 versus 20. Provision was higher as a result of reserves built given the macroeconomic deterioration experienced in the first part of the year. This also reflects the new CISO accounting rules which were adopted as of January 1st of 2020. But as the macroeconomic outlook improved, we released some reserves in the fourth quarter. As we look at share count, it declines 7%, driven by the momentum of the share spot as we move into the second half of 2019 and end in the first quarter of 2020 prior to the time of suspending share repurchases. With $36 billion of excess capital above our common CET1 minimum requirements and excess capital above the SLR reverting back to its normal calculation and completion of the CCAR exam, we'll once again begin repurchasing shares starting today. As you know, our first priority for use of all our capital is to grow our business organically, and we have funded growth in many areas. We have funded and expanded minimum wages to $20 an hour for all our teammates. We expanded and increased COVID benefits, and we've taken care of all that. Now we're looking to return as much capital to our shareholders as we're allowed and as our board deems prudent. So you saw this morning at the beginning of that in a separate press release that our board has approved share repurchase in the first quarter of up to $3.2 billion, including shares issued to employees. This is in addition to maintaining our quarterly dividend at 18 cents per quarter, and that accounts for the return of another $1.6 billion of capital. This is the maximum allowed under the Fed's guidelines established for the first quarter of 2021. Beyond the first quarter, when we find out what the rules are, we'll continue to change our authorizations to reflect those rules. You can see this on slide three. This chart shows solid lines reflecting cumulative change for the year in spending. The dotted line shows the year-over-year change for each month during the year in total spending. Consumer payment activity began and ended the year very strong. In the first two months of the year, payments were up high single digits year-over-year. By April, given the early spread of the pandemic and the full across-the-board economic lockdowns, which is different in the status we are now, payments dropped, and we're down 26%. As some of those funds were depleted and ran off, and the volumes, in fact, grew back to normal levels, we saw a slowdown in the rate of the recovery. This is outside of just debit and credit spending habits, which tend to get all the discussion because they're easy to track, quite frankly. But they represent 75% of the transaction volume, but only about 20% of the dollar volume of transactions. And you can see that they make up that smaller amount on the lower left-hand side. And especially as travel and entertainment spending has shifted away, you've actually even seen debit spending outgrow credit spending. So 80% of the dollar volume of payments made by our consumers happens through person-to-person payments, person-to-business payments, ACH, wires, and many other means, including cash taken out of the ATMs and spent and checks written. So in terms of transaction, you can see at the bottom right of this chart, how the physical payments of cash and checks have moved to more digital forms, which creates operational efficiencies for us and has been a strategic initiative for many years and one that was moved forward by the crisis. Full year 2020 cash and check transaction volume fell to lowest on record, down 21%, as COVID accelerated the migration to digital card-based payments. 2021 has begun as a strong year for payment. The new stimulus checks started hitting customers' accounts in the first weeks of January. More than $11 million of those payments have hit our accounts, about $11 billion, and they've flowed into the accounts, mostly from digital transfers to IRS. So how have payments performed in the first half of January? The first half of January, across all these payment types, is up 6.7% from 2020. In good news, debit and credit is up 5.6%. Growth rates in total exceed pre-COVID levels of growth rates, and there are larger dollar amounts, so bigger dollars and faster growth rates. And that is with about 30% of the $600 payments being spent by our primary checking customers, so 70% more to be spent. As we move to slide four, we can see the activity on the commercial side. In the closing weeks of 2020, we continue to see some stabilization, mainly driven by our middle market auto finance clients as inventories have gotten low and they rebuilt them. As you recall, in the first quarter of the year, we experienced a heightened level of client draws on commitments as the panic borrowing set in with a crisis. and that was about three years of normalized commercial loan growth in a single month.
